title: Vitamin D Supplementation and Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes
authors: Pittas AG, Dawson-Hughes B, Sheehan P, Ware JH, Knowler WC, Aroda VR, et al.
population: US adults at high risk for type 2 diabetes (prediabetes) at 22 academic centres, not selected for vitamin D insufficiency; out-of-trial vitamin D limited to 1000 IU/day
funder: Planning: NIDDK planning grant U34DK091958 and the NIDDK Intramural Research Program. Conduct: NIDDK and the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements through cooperative agreement U01DK098245, which makes the NIDDK project scientist a member of the D2d Research Group; secondary funding from the American Diabetes Association (1-14-D2d-01). The protocol was designed by the planning committee and the primary sponsor (NIDDK) without input from manufacturers; the coordinating-centre statistical team analysed the data.
inKindSupport: Trial pills were purchased from an independent nutritional-supplement manufacturer with no association with members of the research group.
authorConflicts: Dawson-Hughes: grant support from Pfizer and DSM; Ceglia: grant support from DSM; several other authors report fees or grants from pharmaceutical companies.
result: Vitamin D3 4000 IU/day (n=1211) against placebo (n=1212): diabetes in 293 against 323 participants (9.39 against 10.66 per 100 person-years), HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.04). Mean 25-hydroxyvitamin D 27.7 ng/ml at baseline and 54.3 ng/ml at 24 months with vitamin D, 28.8 ng/ml with placebo. Post hoc, baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 12 ng/ml (103 participants): HR 0.38 (0.18 to 0.80); 12 ng/ml or higher (2319): HR 0.92 (0.78 to 1.08). Protocol-specified adverse events, participants with at least one: hypercalcaemia 5 against 3; nephrolithiasis (participant-reported) 24 against 20; serious adverse events 173 against 153; deaths 5 against 5. 24-hour urine calcium was not measured.
